subject: system-design
title: Maintainability
summary: Most of a system's cost comes after launch — maintainability is designing so the people who keep it running, understand it, and change it have an easy time.

blocks.text: A system is written once but lived with for years. The majority of its total cost isn't the initial build — it's the ongoing work of operating, debugging, adapting, and extending it. Maintainability is designing to minimize that long tail of pain.
Maintainability breaks down into three concerns, each aimed at a different audience and a different moment in the system's life.

items: Operability — make it easy to run: good defaults, health checks, and runbooks so operators aren't fighting the system.
Simplicity — make it easy to understand: manage complexity so a new engineer can build an accurate mental model.
Evolvability — make it easy to change: structure the system so new requirements don't demand a rewrite.

blocks.text: Operability is about giving operations a smooth path. That means visibility into runtime behavior, predictable failure modes, and the ability to deploy, roll back, and patch without ceremony. A system you can't observe is a system you can't operate.

Complexity is what makes a system hard to reason about, and reasoning is where bugs hide. The cure is good abstractions — clean contracts that hide internals — and removing incidental moving parts. The goal isn't fewer features; it's less complexity per feature.

blocks.title: Simplicity is a feature
blocks.text: Distinguish essential complexity, which the problem demands, from accidental complexity, which you added. Accidental complexity is the enemy — every line you don't write is a line you don't maintain.

Requirements never sit still, so the system must bend. Good abstractions make change local — you swap an implementation without touching callers — and observability turns 'is the change safe?' into a question you can answer with data rather than hope. Together they let a system grow without seizing up.
